To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
inadequate approaches to trial design and execution, particularly those representing inadequate concealment of treatment allocation, are associated with biased estimates of treatment effects.
inadequate approaches to randomization and blinding in controlled trials are associated with evidence that the trials' results have been biased.
trials in which authors report inadequate concealment or lack of blinding yield estimates of treatment effects that are larger than those in adequately concealed trials and double blind trials.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to improve the quality and reporting of clinical trials.

the quality of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR), and in particular the relationship between the quality of RCTs and estimates of treatment effects.
the question of whether the methodological quality and design of randomized controlled trials is related to the estimates of treatment effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
inadequate allocation concealment is associated with exaggerated estimates of treatment effects, but the magnitude of the effect is uncertain.
inadequate allocation concealment is a potential source of bias, but that the evidence is inconclusive as to whether inadequate allocation concealment actually results in bias.

the results of a randomized trial are valid only if allocation concealment is adequate and that the trial is adequately blinded, and that the trial should not have excluded any participants after randomization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results of the studies are biased in favor of the intervention.
we have shown that inadequate methodological quality is associated with bias, but we have not been able to determine the direction of causality.
there was a 41% exaggeration of the effect size for inadequately controlled trials, and a 30% exaggeration for trials with unclear allocation concealment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the best way to avoid the problem of bias is to do a good job of randomization, blinding, and follow up.
the best evidence for treatment effectiveness comes from well designed and executed randomized controlled trials.
readers of trial reports should not accept at face value any claims of effectiveness.
